name: The Harmony Grove Cucumber Magnolia

location.address: Harmony Grove Cemetery, 30 Grove Street, Salem, MA 01970

official_register.name: Massachusetts DCR Champion Trees 2026 (state champion, rank 1 cucumber magnolia)

access: Free. Cemetery grounds open to visitors 7 am to 7 pm June to September, 7 am to sunset October to May (harmonygrovesalem.org). Tree is at the cemetery entrance on Grove Street.
transport: MBTA commuter rail from Boston North Station to Salem, about 30 minutes, then about 1.5 km on foot west to the cemetery's Grove Street entrance.

location_site.name: Harmony Grove Cemetery entrance, Grove Street

pin_source: Nominatim geocode of DCR address 30 Grove Street (building at the cemetery entrance), 2026-11-03; register note says the tree is at the entrance
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, a cucumber magnolia about 31 metres tall with a trunk 4.7 metres round. It stands at the Grove Street entrance of Harmony Grove Cemetery.
verify_notes: DCR champion row: Magnolia acuminata, 185 in circumference (470 cm), 102 ft (31.1 m) tall, crown spread 86 ft, rank 1 (state champion), measured 2024-02-05, note 'At entrance of Harmony Grove Cemetary'. Measurement date inside 2.5 years counts as last seen alive; register-only plus a ground-owner page for access, hence flagged 'register only'. Cucumber magnolia is a southern Appalachian species that rarely grows naturally in New England (Northborough trail document seen in search, pointer only), so this is a planted specimen. No planting date found; no age claimed. Cemetery founded 1840 per Wikipedia (Salem.org says 1839): do not bridge cemetery date to the tree. Web search found no second source naming this tree; WebSearch summary said nothing on it. Rule 10 clear: cemetery open to visitors per owner site.
story:
The biggest cucumber magnolia in Massachusetts stands at a cemetery gate in Salem. The state's champion tree register ranks it first of its kind, and when the measurers came in February 2024 they recorded a trunk 470 centimetres round, a height of 31 metres and a crown spreading about 26 metres. For a tree most people walking past could not name, that is a great deal of tree.

It is also a long way from home. Cucumber magnolia belongs to the forests of the southern Appalachians and rarely grows wild in New England, so this one was planted. Nobody has recorded who planted it, or when.

Harmony Grove opened around 1840, with sources split between 1839 and 1840, and the magnolia now marks the way in. It would be tempting to make the tree as old as the cemetery, but nothing we have says so, and an entrance tree can as easily have gone in decades later.

What the record does confirm is that it was alive in 2024. The register is the only source that names it, so its age and its story remain open. If you know when it went into the ground, or who put it there, tell us.

name: The Ropes Mansion Copper Beech

location.address: Ropes Mansion Garden, 318 Essex Street, Salem, MA 01970

official_register.name: Massachusetts DCR Legacy Trees 2026 (European beech, rank 14)

access: Free. The Ropes Mansion Garden (Peabody Essex Museum) is open to the public every day of the year, dawn to dusk, no charge (Salem.org listing). PEM has ropes and signs asking visitors to stay a few steps back from the tree.
transport: MBTA commuter rail from Boston North Station to Salem, about 30 minutes, then about 600 metres on foot to the Ropes Mansion on Essex Street.
pin_source: Nominatim geocode of DCR address (Ropes Mansion building), 2026-11-03
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its purple leaves and the ropes and signs keeping visitors a few steps back. It is the large copper beech in the Ropes Mansion garden, behind the house on Essex Street.
verify_notes: Two sources. DCR: Fagus sylvatica, 198 in (503 cm), 77.5 ft (23.6 m), spread 81.5 ft, rank 14, measured 2026-01-08 (alive this year). PEM (owner of the garden) blog on its arboretum certification: 'the 100-year-old copper beech tree at the Ropes Mansion', 'planted in 1913', 'visible as a ten-year-old sapling in an archival photograph', 'probably given to John Robinson by Charles Sprague Sargent, the first director of the Arnold Arboretum, as part of a gift of 91 woody plants'. About four years before the post it had a Ganoderma (gianoderma in the post) fungal infection; this year tests showed the fungus stopped progressing; it does not currently have to come down. A branch holds a foot-deep pocket of water that may hold back the fungus. Garden laid out in 1912 by Salem botanist John Robinson. Salem Inn gives a different story (transplanted from the Arnold Arboretum in 1913); PEM says probably a gift from Sargent; not settled. PEM also gives conflicting ages (100-year-old vs 'at least 120' in a search snippet that was not seen on the fetched page, so ignore). Assumption to flag: the DCR row 'Beech, European, Ropes Mansion, 318 Essex St' is taken to be this copper beech; PEM names only one beech there but does not cite the register. Blog date uncertain, photo captioned 2024.
story:
A pocket of water a foot deep, held in one of its branches, may be part of what is keeping this beech alive. Some years ago the Peabody Essex Museum, which looks after the Ropes Mansion garden, found a Ganoderma fungus at work in the tree. Later tests showed the infection had stopped spreading, and the museum thinks the standing water may be helping to hold it back. For now the tree does not have to come down.

It went into the garden in 1913, a year after the Salem botanist John Robinson laid the garden out, and an archival photograph shows it as a ten-year-old sapling. The museum says it was probably one of 91 woody plants that Charles Sprague Sargent of the Arnold Arboretum gave to Robinson. A local inn tells it differently, as a tree transplanted from the Arboretum that year. The two accounts are close but not the same, and neither is settled.

The state's legacy tree register lists a European beech at the Ropes Mansion with a trunk 503 centimetres round, 23.6 metres tall and a crown about 25 metres across, measured in January 2026. The museum names only one beech in the garden, so this is taken to be it.

Ropes and signs now ask visitors to stay a few steps back from it.

name: The Broad Street Cemetery White Oak

location.address: Broad Street Cemetery, Broad Street, Salem, MA 01970

official_register.name: Massachusetts DCR Legacy Trees 2026 (white oak, rank 13)

access: Free; a city-owned historic burying ground (second-oldest in Salem, 2.69 acres per Find a Grave) listed by Destination Salem as a place to visit, across from the Pickering House. Posted hours not found.
transport: MBTA commuter rail from Boston North Station to Salem, about 30 minutes, then about 1 km on foot south to Broad Street.
pin_source: Nominatim geocode of the cemetery polygon centroid, 2026-11-03; register location text 'towards the center'
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big white oak among the headstones, about 4.4 metres round and broader than it is tall. It stands towards the centre of the small Broad Street Cemetery.
verify_notes: DCR: Quercus alba, 172 in (437 cm), 57 ft (17.4 m), spread 63.75 ft, rank 13, measured 2026-01-08 (alive this year), location text 'Broad St Cemetery, towards the center'. The ground is small (2.69 acres), so the small-site rule fits. Register only plus a Salem.org page for access: flagged 'register only'. Cemetery established 1655 (Salem.org); do NOT bridge this to the oak's age. No age basis; leave to the reader. Stout rather than tall (17 m) for a 437 cm white oak, which fits an open-grown crown. Public access not stated in words by any page; inferred from Salem.org listing it as a cemetery to visit and from guided tours (Salem Historical Society 2019 listing seen in search).
story:
Salem's second-oldest burying ground holds a white oak nearly four and a half metres round, and no record says how long it has been there. The state's legacy tree register measured it in January 2026 at 437 centimetres around the trunk and placed it thirteenth among the white oaks on its list for Massachusetts.

It is not a tall tree. At 17.4 metres it is stout rather than lofty, with a crown about 19 metres wide, the shape you would expect of an oak that grew up in the open. The register places it towards the centre of the cemetery, a small ground of under three acres across the road from the Pickering House.

The Broad Street Cemetery dates from 1655, which makes an obvious story tempting. Nothing we have says the oak is anywhere near that old, and the cemetery's founding tells us nothing about when the tree took root. Girth alone is a poor clock for an open-grown oak, and no planting date has turned up.

So the honest answer is that its age is unknown. If you know more, from a family record, an old photograph of the cemetery or a local history, tell us.

name: The Morell House Sycamore

location.address: 627 Massachusetts Avenue, Lexington, MA 02420 (front of house, beside the house sign)

official_register.name: Massachusetts DCR Legacy Trees 2026 (American sycamore, rank 10)

access: View-only from the public pavement on Massachusetts Avenue; the house is a private address, do not enter the grounds.
transport: MBTA Red Line to Alewife, then bus 62 or 76 along Massachusetts Avenue into East Lexington; the tree is in front of number 627.
pin_source: Nominatim geocode of the DCR address (Obadiah Parker - N. Ambrose Morell House building), 2026-11-03; pin belongs on the street in front
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, a sycamore 28 metres tall with a crown about 30 metres wide. It stands in front of 627 Massachusetts Avenue, beside the historic house sign, seen from the pavement.
verify_notes: One source: DCR Legacy row, Platanus occidentalis (the register cell is garbled 'Platanus┬áoccidentalis'), 191 in (485 cm), 93 ft (28.3 m), crown spread 100 ft, rank 10, measured 2025-08-08 (alive last year). Register note: 'next to Morell-Dana house sign', location text '627 Massachusetts Avenue ... front of house'. OSM geocode names the building 'Obadiah Parker - N. Ambrose Morell House' (a historic inventory house). Street visibility is inferred from the register note (front of house, beside a sign facing the road), not seen on imagery; if a reviewer can confirm on street-level imagery, drop the flag. House is private: no walking in. Another Lexington DCR row (European beech, 237 in, rank 5, 2025) has location withheld (null): not usable. No age basis. Nothing ties it to 1775.
story:
This sycamore is 28 metres tall and its crown is wider still, about 30 metres from side to side. The state's legacy tree register measured it in August 2025 with a trunk 485 centimetres round and ranked it tenth among the American sycamores on its Massachusetts list. It stands in the front garden of 627 Massachusetts Avenue in East Lexington, beside the sign of a historic house that maps name after Obadiah Parker and N. Ambrose Morell.

The house is a private home, so this is a tree to look at from the pavement. The register's note puts it at the front of the house, next to the house sign on the main road, which means it should be plain from the street. Stay on the public side and do not go onto the grounds.

Lexington is a town where a great deal is dated to 1775, and it would be easy to hang this tree on that year. Nothing we have connects it to 1775 or to any other date. Its age is not recorded, and a trunk this size, on its own, does not settle it.

The register is the only source for this tree, and its view from the street rests on the register's description rather than on a photograph. If you pass it and can confirm it, or know its history, tell us.
